assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment is merged into 'Table 1: Shipment Grouping Decision' alongside destination and availability, not its own table.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: Delivery address columns appear only inside the combined 'Table 1: Shipment Grouping Decision', not a separate table.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: Availability columns are part of the same merged 'Table 1: Shipment Grouping Decision', not isolated in their own table.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: ## Table 2: Warehouse Allocation to Minimize Shipments

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Rows: 'Both pickup, same store' (Home Delivery both), 'Both pickup, same store' (Pickup both), 'Pickup and delivery mixed' (mix).

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: 'Both delivered to the same address...' and 'Gift order, two delivery addresses' rows in Table 1.

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: Rows: 'Both in stock', 'One item in stock, one on backorder', 'Two backorder items, different expected dates', plus open question 1 on pre-order/backorder equivalence.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: No scenario explicitly compares a feasible fewer-warehouse split against a more-warehouse alternative to show preference for fewer warehouses.

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Table 3 has only 'shared warehouse', 'different single warehouses', and 'multiple shared warehouses (tie)' rows; no 'companion not available anywhere' scenario.

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: 'Both delivered to the same address, both in stock', 'Pickup and delivery mixed, regardless of availability'

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Columns 'Item A Fulfillment | Item A Destination | Item A Availability | Item B Fulfillment | Item B Destination | Item B Availability' keep per-item properties distinct

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Table 2 uses 'Order Quantity' column: '| Order Quantity | Stock by Warehouse | Ships From? | Shipment Count? |'

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Columns like 'Stock by Warehouse', 'Ships From?', 'Shipment Count?' use business language

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: 'Same Shipment? | Reason?' and 'Ships From? | Shipment Count?' and 'Ship Together?'

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: 'Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3, Chicago: 0 | Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3 | 2' matches stock exactly

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.

Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 merges fulfillment, destination, and availability splitting into one 'Shipment Grouping Decision' table instead of three separate concern tables as expected

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Table 1 needs 9 rows varying fulfillment/destination/availability together since concerns weren't separated, e.g. rows for pickup vs delivery mixed with availability sets
